definitions.type: compact additive group with normalized measure
definitions.definition: torus=ℝ/(2πℤ), written \mathbb T in formulas; integration uses dx/(2π). The parameter T denotes the time horizon.

definitions.type: Fourier coefficient map on the torus
definitions.definition: For integrable f, Fourier(f)(k) = fhat(k) = (2 pi)^(-1) integral_0^{2 pi} f(x) exp(-ikx) dx; extend by distributional duality.

For real s, H^s is the completion of trigonometric polynomials with norm squared sum_{k in Z} <k>^(2s)|fhat(k)|^2, <k>=(1+k^2)^(1/2). Negative spaces are distributions. L2=H^0 with normalized measure. On mean-zero distributions dot H^s has squared norm sum_{k!=0}|k|^(2s)|fhat(k)|^2. Smooth means spatially C-infinity. Real means fhat(-k)=conjugate(fhat(k)), and mean-zero means fhat(0)=0. Sequence ell2 uses counting measure. Time L-infinity norms are essential suprema, except time suprema of continuous representatives. Generic constants C may change; C_M depends only on gamma,T,M, never on a Fourier support bound or timestep.

definitions.type: Airy group indexed by real times
definitions.definition: S_t = exp(-t partial_x^3); Fourier(S_t f)(k)= exp(it k^3) fhat(k).
P0 f=fhat(0), as a constant function.
P=I-P0; the identity operator is I.

definitions.type: inverse spatial derivative with zero mode removed
definitions.definition: Dinv=partial_x^(-1)=D^(-1), Fourier multiplier (ik)^(-1) at nonzero k and zero at k=0.

definitions.type: time-integrated trilinear operator initially on smooth inputs
definitions.definition: C_I(f,g,h)= integral_I S_{-t}P{P[(S_t f)(S_t g)](S_t Dinv h)} dt. For lower regularity its meaning is the bounded extension supplied by the continuous estimates.

For compact interval I, ||f||_{X(I)}=||f||_{L-infinity(I;L2)}+||partial_t f||_{L-infinity(I;H^(-pstar))}, using the distributional time derivative. Subintervals use the same continuous representatives; piecewise smooth continuous functions have this distributional derivative almost everywhere.
a_gamma=1/2-gamma if 0<gamma<1/2, a_gamma=1/8 if gamma=1/2, and a_gamma=0 if 1/2<gamma<=1.
For time-independent mean-zero f and t in I_n=[t_n,t_n+tau], F_n(t;f)=1/2 integral_{t_n}^t B_s(f,f) ds. Write F_n(t)=F_n(t;f) when f is fixed.

inputs.statement: Li–Wu continuous trilinear estimates: Let 0<=lambda<=1, b>=a>=0, b-a<=1, and f_j in L-infinity([a,b];H^lambda), partial_t f_j in L-infinity([a,b];H^(-23/14)), j=1,2,3. The operator C_[a,b] of D019 satisfies ||C_[a,b](f1,f2,f3)||_{L2} <= C(b-a) product_j ||f_j||_{X([a,b])}+C||f_i||_{L-infinity H^(-23/14)} product_{j!=i}||f_j||_{L-infinity L2}, for each i=1,2,3. If all inputs are time-independent, ||C_[a,b](f1,f2,f3)||_{L2}<=C_lambda(b-a)^lambda product_j||f_j||_{H^lambda}. In this source statement all spatial norms are Li–Wu's unnormalized norms, equal to sqrt(2 pi) times D003 norms, including X. Constants are independent of the time location and Fourier support.

inputs.statement: Li–Wu product and bilinear-stage estimates: For 0<lambda<=1 define a(lambda)=1/2-lambda if lambda<1/2, any fixed positive epsilon if lambda=1/2, and 0 if lambda>1/2. Then ||fg||_2<=C_lambda,epsilon ||f||_{H^lambda}||g||_{H^{a(lambda)}}. For mean-zero time-independent f1,f2 in H^lambda and a step [t_n,t_n+tau] with tau>0, the bilinear stage G_n(t;f1,f2)=(1/2) integral_{t_n}^t B_s(f1,f2) ds satisfies ||G_n(t;f1,f2)||_{H^beta}<=C tau^((1+lambda-beta)/(1+lambda-beta0))||f1||_{H^lambda}||f2||_{H^lambda}, beta0<=beta<=1+lambda, uniformly on the step. Here beta0=2lambda-3/2 if lambda<1/2, beta0=-1/2-epsilon if lambda=1/2 with an arbitrary fixed sufficiently small epsilon>0, and beta0=lambda-1 if lambda>1/2. All source spatial norms are sqrt(2 pi) times ours; constants depend on exponents and chosen epsilon but not on n,tau or support.

argument.text: Use H001. For E002 take arbitrary I=[a,b] with 0<=a<=b and b-a<=1 and lambda=0 for the X estimate. X gives precisely L-infinity L2 and L-infinity H^(-23/14) derivative, its hypotheses. Its three choices of negative-norm slot are retained. For constant inputs use E002 with any lambda in [0,1]. Each source spatial norm is sqrt(2 pi) times ours: divide by sqrt(2 pi) on the output and absorb the remaining product factors 2 pi into the constant. This proves the first two assertions without changing their exponent or time length. Smooth or continuous piecewise smooth time functions have the stated distributional derivative, so E002 applies directly. General X inputs use the source bounded interpretation of the operator. When a=b the integral is zero, so the zero-length interval case follows directly.

For time-independent fj in H^lambda and 0<=lambda<=1, ||C_I(f1,f2,f3)||_2<=C_lambda |I|^lambda product_j||fj||_{H^lambda}; at |I|=0 the integral is zero. Constants are uniform in interval location and support, and the bounded interpretation agrees with smooth inputs.

argument.text:
For the product and stages use E003 with lambda=gamma and epsilon=1/8 at gamma=1/2. The diagonal bilinear stage is exactly F_n(t;w), by definition. The necessary source exponent checks and retained calculations are:
when \(\|w\|_{H^\gamma}\le M\). One can take \(a_\gamma=1/2-\gamma\) for \(0<\gamma<1/2\), \(1/8\) for \(\gamma=1/2\), and \(a_\gamma=0\) for \(\gamma>1/2\). For clarity, the source stage exponent is \(\theta=(1+\gamma-\beta)/(1+\gamma-\beta_0)\), with \(\beta_0=2\gamma-3/2\) for \(0<\gamma<1/2\), \(\beta_0=-1/2-\epsilon\) for \(\gamma=1/2\), and \(\beta_0=\gamma-1\) for \(1/2<\gamma\le1\). Take \(\epsilon=1/8\) in the middle case. At \(\beta=a_\gamma\) the exponents are respectively \((1/2+2\gamma)/(5/2-\gamma)\ge\gamma\), \(11/17>1/2\) and \((1+\gamma)/2\ge\gamma\). Every \(a_\gamma\) lies in the source interval \([\beta_0,1+\gamma]\). Since \(0<\tau\le1\), these exponents imply the first bound in the asserted stage inequalities. At \(\beta=1+\gamma\) the exponent is zero, giving the second. The product inequality is E003, with the same fixed \(1/8\) choice when \(\gamma=1/2\). Source \(L^2\) and \(H^s\) norms are \(\sqrt{2\pi}\) times ours; dividing the source inequalities absorbs only fixed factors into constants. These estimates require no regularity beyond \(H^\gamma\) on \(w\). For the first range the exponent inequality reduces to gamma^2-gamma/2+1/2=(gamma-1/4)^2+7/16>0; at gamma=1/2 the exponent is 11/17 and in the last range (1+gamma)/2>=gamma. Thus both stage conclusions follow uniformly for 0<tau<=1. All relevant bounds and the product inequality have now been proved in the declared normalization.
